blocks.text: A decoder model generates text one token at a time, each new token predicted using only the tokens that came before it, never the tokens that come after, since those have not been generated yet.

This one directional, causal view is the defining feature of decoder models, and it is the architecture behind essentially every modern conversational large language model, including the ones most fine-tuning projects today actually train.
1. What a Decoder Model Actually Does

blocks.alt: What a Decoder Model Actually Does
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216685-865107352.png

Given a sequence of tokens so far, a decoder model predicts the single most likely next token, then that predicted token gets added to the sequence, and the process repeats, generating text one token at a time.
This is fundamentally different from an encoder, which sees the full input at once and produces representations, a decoder builds its output incrementally, step by step.
2. Causal Masking, The Defining Trait
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216685-150304282.png

When a decoder processes a position in the sequence, it is deliberately prevented from looking at any token that comes after it, a restriction called causal masking, since at generation time those future tokens genuinely do not exist yet.

This causal constraint is exactly what makes decoder models useful for generation, they learn to predict what comes next given only what came before, which is precisely the situation they face when actually generating text.
3. Autoregressive Generation, One Token at a Time

blocks.alt: Autoregressive Generation, One Token at a Time
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216685-958507783.png

The word autoregressive describes exactly this process, each new token is predicted based on the tokens generated so far, then fed back in as part of the input for predicting the next one, repeating until the response is complete.
This loop is why generating a long response takes proportionally longer than generating a short one, each additional token requires another full pass through the model.
4. A Concrete Architecture Example, GPT Style Models

blocks.alt: A Concrete Architecture Example, GPT Style Models
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448352631-645854604.png

The GPT family of models popularized the decoder only architecture at scale, stacking many decoder layers, each refining the representation used to predict the next token, trained purely on the objective of predicting what word comes next across a massive amount of text.
Nearly every widely used conversational assistant today, regardless of the company that built it, follows this same fundamental decoder only shape.
5. Why Nearly Every Modern LLM Is Decoder Only

blocks.alt: Why Nearly Every Modern LLM Is Decoder Only
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448352632-673327126.png

A decoder only model can be framed to handle almost any task, answering questions, writing code, summarizing, translating, simply by changing the prompt, since generation itself is flexible enough to produce any kind of text output.

This flexibility is a major reason the field converged heavily toward decoder only architectures, one general purpose generation mechanism instead of separate specialized architectures for every different kind of task.

blocks.text: 6. Decoder Models and Next Token Prediction

blocks.alt: Decoder Models and Next Token Prediction
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448352633-175009864.png

Decoder models are pretrained using next token prediction, given the text so far, predict the next word, a simple objective that, applied across a huge and varied corpus, produces surprisingly broad language understanding and reasoning ability.

blocks.title: The same objective, at two very different scales
blocks.content: Pretraining runs next token prediction across trillions of tokens, while fine-tuning often continues that same basic objective on a much smaller, task specific dataset.

blocks.text: 7. What Decoder Models Are Good At

Decoder models excel at any task framed as producing new text, writing, summarizing, answering, translating, or generating code, since generation is exactly what their architecture and training objective are built around.

code.content:
# A simplified autoregressive generation loop
tokens = tokenize(prompt)
for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
    next_token = decoder_model.predict_next(tokens)
    tokens.append(next_token)
    if next_token == end_of_sequence_token:
        break
response = detokenize(tokens)

blocks.text: 8. Fine-Tuning a Decoder Model
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448352633-209832514.png

Fine-tuning a decoder model usually means continuing its next token prediction training on examples that demonstrate the specific style, format, or task you want, so the model default generation behavior shifts toward those examples.

This is the most common fine-tuning scenario covered throughout the rest of this course, since decoder only models are what nearly every modern large language model, and therefore nearly every fine-tuning project, is actually built on.
9. Decoder Models as the Default Fine-Tuning Target

Given how dominant decoder only architectures have become for general purpose language models, the vast majority of fine-tuning techniques covered later in this course, supervised fine-tuning, LoRA, alignment training, assume a decoder model as the starting point.

Encoder models still matter for specific classification and retrieval tasks, but decoder models are the default target when the goal is a model that writes, converses, or generates any kind of new content.
Worked Example

A team wants a model that drafts product descriptions in a specific brand voice given a short list of product features. They start from a pretrained decoder only model and fine-tune it on two thousand examples pairing feature lists with correctly written descriptions.

Because the decoder model was already pretrained on next token prediction across huge amounts of general text, it already knows how to write fluent language, fine-tuning simply redirects that ability toward this specific writing task and voice, producing a model that generates on-brand descriptions by default.
Common Mistakes

items: Expecting a decoder model to see future tokens the way an encoder model does, when causal masking specifically prevents that
Choosing an encoder model for a task that actually requires generating new text
Underestimating how generation time scales with response length, since each token requires another pass through the model
Forgetting that fine-tuning a decoder model still relies on the same next token prediction mechanism used in pretraining

blocks.text: Practice

Take a task you want a model to perform, and check whether it fundamentally requires generating new text. If it does, that is a strong signal you want a decoder model as your fine-tuning target, the case for the vast majority of fine-tuning projects in practice.
Key Takeaway

Decoder models generate text one token at a time using only past context, trained through next token prediction, and this autoregressive, decoder only architecture is the foundation behind nearly every modern large language model and the vast majority of fine-tuning projects covered in this course.
